common_name: Walken Oat (Tall Late-Maturing Forage and Cover Crop Oat)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in fall; Walken is an extra-tall, late-maturing white oat prized for heavy forage production.

directions: Walken is an old University of Kentucky-released white oat grown almost exclusively for forage rather than grain, valued for its unusually tall growth and heavy straw strength. Drill or broadcast in fall so plants establish before the coldest weather, since its maturity runs two to three weeks later than standard winter oats like Nora. The long growing season and vigorous late growth make it a strong choice for grazing, hay, or silage, and as a cover crop it produces substantial biomass to protect soil through winter. Mow, graze, or terminate before seed set if using it strictly as a soil-building cover.
sources: Oregon State University winter oat variety trials

common_name: CDC Baler Oat (Tall Leafy Western Canadian Forage Oat)

planting.note: Drill in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; CDC Baler is bred for a dense, leafy canopy and high silage yield.

directions: CDC Baler is a Canadian-bred forage oat developed at the Crop Development Centre for tall growth, a dense leaf canopy, and strong standability under heavy biomass. Drill in early spring in cool regions where it is used for silage, swath grazing, or combined plantings with annual forage peas. Its dense stand and rapid early growth make it an effective weed-suppressing cover as well, and it reliably outperforms shorter oat varieties for total forage tonnage. Cut or terminate at the boot-to-heading stage for the best balance of yield and feed quality.
sources: Peace Country Beef & Forage Association variety trials

common_name: ForagePlus Oat (Late-Heading High-Yield Wisconsin Forage Oat)

planting.note: Drill in early spring; ForagePlus heads 5-7 days later than standard forage oats, giving an extended vegetative window before heading.

directions: ForagePlus was released by the University of Wisconsin-Madison specifically for silage and baleage production, with a notably later heading date than companion varieties like Ensiler and Belle that extends the window of high-quality vegetative growth. Drill in early spring for spring-sown forage, where its late maturity allows a longer harvest flexibility without a steep quality drop-off. As a cover crop, the extended vegetative stage builds more standing biomass before stem elongation, giving extra weeks of living soil cover compared to earlier-heading oats. It also carries good resistance to crown rust, a common late-season problem in humid regions.
sources: University of Wisconsin-Madison Wisconsin Crop Improvement Association

subcategory: winter annual cover/forage cereal grain hybrid

planting.note: Drill into a prepared fall seedbed; Forerunner's facultative growth habit also allows spring sowing where winters are too severe for fall establishment.

directions: Forerunner is an awnless triticale bred to remove the bristly awns found on most cereal grains, making it safer and more comfortable to handle as baled hay or silage. Its facultative growth habit means it is not strictly locked into a fall-only or spring-only planting pattern, giving growers flexibility depending on regional winters. As a cover crop it produces substantial fibrous root mass and vegetative biomass, helping capture residual soil nitrogen and build organic matter when turned under as green manure. Mow or terminate at the boot-to-early-heading stage for the best forage quality, or let it stand longer for maximum soil-building biomass.
sources: Washington State Crop Improvement Association variety data sheet

common_name: NE426GT Triticale (High-Yield Nebraska Grain and Forage Triticale)
subcategory: winter annual cover/forage cereal grain hybrid

planting.note: Drill in early fall; NE426GT is an early-heading winter triticale valued for combining high grain yield with good fall forage production.

directions: NE426GT was released by the University of Nebraska and Iowa State University as a dual-purpose winter triticale, selected for very high grain yield alongside solid fall forage production. Drill into a fall seedbed early enough for plants to tiller and build fall forage before dormancy, since its early-heading habit lets it be grazed or clipped in fall without compromising the following grain or cover-crop benefit. It carries moderate resistance to stem and leaf rust, helping maintain stand health through a long growing season. Where grown purely as a cover crop, its awned, high-biomass growth habit still scavenges nitrogen and protects soil over winter even without harvesting the grain.
sources: University of Nebraska-Lincoln Agricultural Research Division
Iowa State University small grains breeding program

common_name: Exceed BMR Pearl Millet (Brown Midrib Drought-Tolerant Forage Millet)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm; Exceed BMR carries the brown midrib trait for notably higher forage digestibility than standard pearl millet.

directions: Exceed BMR is a hybrid pearl millet carrying the brown midrib (BMR) gene, which lowers lignin content and makes its forage substantially more digestible than conventional pearl millet types. Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger passes, since pearl millet seed rots quickly in cold, wet ground. It tolerates drought well and regrows vigorously after grazing or mowing, making it useful both as a high-quality summer forage and as a fast-establishing warm-season cover that shades out weeds and builds organic matter. Begin grazing or cutting once plants reach roughly two feet tall and allow adequate regrowth between cuttings; frost will terminate the stand at season's end.
